Field surveys of the coral-dwelling Ring-eye pygmygoby, Trimma benjamini, have clarified several fundamental life-history parameters for this diminutive goby. Newly hatched larvae emerge from their demersal eggs after an incubation period of approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days] when maintained at a constant water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. At the moment of eclosion, these prolarvae carry a minuscule wet weight of roughly 0.0002771 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.0002771 grams], a value reflecting the modest dimensions of the yolk-laden ovum. This initial mass is consistent with the extremely small body size that characterizes the entire genus. The protracted embryonic development relative to egg size may relate to the stable thermal regime of the shallow-reef habitats this species occupies, where temperatures typically hover near 27.7 °C for much of the year.

Juveniles of Trimma benjamini undergo a period of rapid somatic growth following the onset of exogenous feeding, which commences after the yolk-sac larva has fully utilized its endogenous reserves. During this sub-adult phase, individuals achieve a total length of 1.5 centimeters [Lp = 1.5 centimeters] at the point of sexual maturation, which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 0.0146 grams [Wwp = 0.0146 grams]. This length-based threshold for reproductive activation is notably small even among gobies, highlighting the species' extremely compressed life-history schedule. The allometric relationship linking length to mass in these developing fish follows a typical power-law trajectory, with the pubertal mass representing just over ten percent of the maximum adult wet weight eventually attained later in life.

Reproductively active adults of this species exhibit a surprisingly high annual reproductive output given their diminutive stature. Field observations indicate that mature females produce approximately 1 egg per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1 egg per clutch], with multiple clutches laid over the spawning season totaling approximately 357 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 357 clutches per year] when reared under a stable thermal regime of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a value that approaches the theoretical maximum for a fish of this body size. This high fecundity is sustained through quasi-continuous batch spawning, a reproductive strategy typical of small-bodied, short-lived teleosts that rely on rapid population replacement to persist in dynamic reef environments.

The ultimate body size attained by fully grown Trimma benjamini adults is remarkably constrained. The maximum total length recorded for this species is 3.0 centimeters [Li = 3.0 centimeters], which corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 0.144 grams [Wwi = 0.144 grams]. This asymptotic size places it among the smallest vertebrate species known, with the entire adult lifespan capable of being completed within a calendar year. The wet weight at birth represents a minuscule fraction of this final adult dimension, emphasizing the extraordinary magnitude of the mass increase—roughly a 520-fold gain—that occurs between the prolarval and adult stages. Reaching such a size plateau likely imposes a strict energetic ceiling on fecundity and may explain the evolution of continuous batch spawning.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of their coral-reef environment, the entire life cycle of Trimma benjamini unfolds rapidly. At a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is 140 days [am = 140 days], making it one of the shortest-lived vertebrates in the Indo-Pacific region. This abbreviated longevity, combined with the approximately 6-day embryonic period (approximately 6 days) [ab = approximately 6 days], produces an extremely compressed generation time at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. The total length at puberty of 1.5 centimeters [Lp = 1.5 centimeters] is reached relatively quickly, and the subsequent adult phase is almost entirely devoted to reproductive effort, with females producing clutches at a frequency of approximately 357 [F_R_i = approximately 357] per year. Such a life-history syndrome—tiny body size, rapid maturation, semelparous-like investment, and short lifespan—is an adaptation to the high mortality rates and patchy habitat availability of shallow coral-reef ecosystems.
